titre: Du Bois and the First Urban Sociological Survey
accroche: In 1896, a young sociology PhD moves into a Black neighborhood of Philadelphia to interview, door to door, more than five thousand people.
contenu_vulgarise:
In August 1896, W. E. B. Du Bois, twenty-eight years old and, the year before, the first African American to earn a doctorate from Harvard, is hired by the University of Pennsylvania as an “assistant in sociology” for one year. His mission: to study the living conditions of the Black population of Philadelphia's Seventh Ward. He moves there with his wife, above the College Settlement, at the corner of Seventh and Lombard Streets.

## The Mechanism

For more than a year, until December 1897, Du Bois conducts the door-to-door survey himself, with a single collaborator, Isabel Eaton. He gathers more than five thousand individual interviews on the occupation, housing, health, education, religious practice, and family life of every household in the ward, which he cross-references with archival records and descriptive statistics. He sorts the results street by street on color-coded maps, by precise social and economic categories: a method that most social surveys of the time, in the United States as in Great Britain, still ignored, preferring impressionistic observation or the statistical aggregate at the scale of an entire city.

Published in 1899 under the title *The Philadelphia Negro: A Social Study*, the 520-page work refuses to explain the poverty, delinquency, or mortality observed in the ward by racial inferiority, an explanation then widespread in American academic circles. Du Bois links them, with figures to back it up, to the legacy of slavery, to hiring discrimination, which shuts skilled Black workers out of most skilled trades, and to housing segregation, which concentrates the Black population in the city's least healthy neighborhoods. It is, according to historians of the discipline, the first sociological case study of a Black community in the United States.

## What It Shifts

The book shifts the question that white America was then asking about its poor Black neighborhoods. It asked: what is it about these populations that explains their condition? Du Bois turns the question back toward institutions: what condition have slavery, hiring, and housing produced? Historians of sociology locate in this survey a decisive step in Du Bois's reformulation of the very notion of race: no longer a biological category that would explain a social destiny, but a social relation that fieldwork can document, neighborhood by neighborhood, household by household. More than a century after its publication, the maps he drew street by street are still cited as one of the first examples of social research based entirely on data that its author collected himself, rather than on a general theory applied to a neighborhood he would never have visited.

repere.texte: Between August 1896 and December 1897, Du Bois gathers more than 5,000 individual interviews, door to door, with a single collaborator, to map street by street the living conditions of Philadelphia's Seventh Ward.
repere.source: W. E. B. Du Bois, The Philadelphia Negro: A Social Study, published for the University of Pennsylvania, 1899

carte.punch: In 1896, a young sociology PhD himself interviews more than 5,000 residents of one neighborhood.
carte.idee: For the University of Pennsylvania, Du Bois surveys a Black neighborhood of Philadelphia door to door for sixteen months. His 1899 book explains the poverty he documents there by slavery, hiring, and housing, and not by the racial inferiority then commonly invoked.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Complete scan, including the maps and the methodological appendices.

quiz.question: How does Du Bois's method in The Philadelphia Negro break with the social surveys of his time?
choix: He relies solely on statistics already published by the city authorities
He entrusts the fieldwork to a team of several dozen assistants recruited locally
He limits his study to a small sample of households drawn at random across the whole city
He himself conducts, with a single collaborator, more than five thousand individual interviews mapped street by street
quiz.explication: Du Bois relies neither on already aggregated statistics, nor on a large team, nor on a sample scattered across the whole city: he himself conducts, with Isabel Eaton, an exhaustive, mapped survey of the Seventh Ward.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What mission does the University of Pennsylvania give Du Bois in 1896?
choix: To head a new department of sociology at the university
To study for a year, as an “assistant in sociology,” the living conditions of the Seventh Ward
To train Philadelphia's municipal investigators in statistical methods
To write a report on all the poor neighborhoods of the entire city
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Hired by the University of Pennsylvania as an “assistant in sociology” for one year, Du Bois is tasked with studying the living conditions of the Black population of the Seventh Ward, not with heading a department, training investigators, or covering the whole city.

quiz_supplementaire.question: To what does Du Bois attribute, with figures to back it up, the poverty and mortality observed in the Seventh Ward?
choix: To racial inferiority, an explanation he takes over from the academic circles of the time
To the neighborhood's climate and population density, which he considers decisive
To the legacy of slavery, hiring discrimination, and housing segregation
To the absence of religious instruction in the neighborhood's families
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Du Bois links, with figures to back it up, the neighborhood's poverty and mortality to the legacy of slavery, hiring discrimination, and housing segregation, and explicitly rejects the explanation by racial inferiority then widespread in academic circles.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to historians of sociology, what conceptual shift does Du Bois make with this survey?
choix: He makes race no longer a biological category but a social relation that fieldwork can document
He demonstrates that urban poverty can never be measured precisely
He establishes that national statistics suffice to understand a neighborhood
He proposes replacing fieldwork with a general theory applicable to any city
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Historians locate in this survey a decisive step in which Du Bois reformulates race, no longer a biological category that would explain a social destiny, but a social relation that fieldwork documents, neighborhood by neighborhood, household by household.
